JWTs, Testing and API Docs for the Final Leg of the Trip

1

JWT Essentials: closing the second named gap

Module 11 deliberately left two things unfinished: plain-text passwords and stub tokens. Module 12 closed the password gap with bcrypt. Module 13 closes the token gap by replacing stub access tokens with real signed JWTs.

Travel checklist for JWTs

IssueUse jwt.sign() to produce a real token with the expected claims.
DecodeHeader and payload are readable without a secret because JWTs are encoded, not encrypted.
Verifyjwt.verify() checks the signature and returns decoded claims.
Differentiate failuresTampering, wrong secret and expiry are not all the same failure mode.

Issuing the token

The real token shape matches the earlier Sprint 6 stub contract: sub for the username and roles for authorization. HS256 is the signing algorithm.

jwt.sign(...) 
const token = jwt.sign(
  {
    sub: "alice",
    roles: ["MISSION_OPERATOR"]
  },
  JWT_SECRET,
  {
    algorithm: "HS256",
    expiresIn: "15m"
  }
);

// header.payload.signature

Decoding is not verifying

Anyone holding the token can read the header and payload. The secret protects integrity, not confidentiality, so a JWT payload must never contain data the holder should not see.

Decoding header + payload 
const [header, payload, signature] =
  token.split(".");

console.log(
  Buffer.from(header, "base64url").toString()
);

console.log(
  Buffer.from(payload, "base64url").toString()
);

// readable without a secret

Verification

jwt.verify() proves the signature was created with the right secret and that the token has not expired. It then returns the decoded claims.

jwt.verify(...) 
const decoded = jwt.verify(token, JWT_SECRET);
console.log(decoded.sub);   // alice
console.log(decoded.roles); // [ 'MISSION_OPERATOR' ]

Three real failure modes

A single-byte change to the header or payload breaks the signature. Wrong secret and tampering both look like signature failure, while expiry has its own named error.

Verification errors 
// tampered payload + old signature
JsonWebTokenError: invalid signature

// wrong secret
JsonWebTokenError: invalid signature

// expired token
TokenExpiredError: jwt expired
Deliberate asymmetry: access tokens become real short-lived JWTs, but refresh tokens stay opaque random strings. That is what makes logout and refresh-token revocation possible without waiting for a JWT expiry.
The secret must match exactly: this service deliberately uses the same JWT_SECRET variable name and fallback string as the earlier auth stub. That shared secret is what allows the unchanged Java mission service to trust tokens from this new Node/NestJS service.
auth.service.ts 
import { Injectable, UnauthorizedException, ConflictException } from "@nestjs/common";
import * as bcrypt from "bcrypt";
import * as jwt from "jsonwebtoken";
import { randomBytes } from "crypto";
import { logAuthEvent } from "./logger";

interface StoredUser {
  passwordHash: string;
  roles: string[];
  refreshToken: string | null;
}

const SALT_ROUNDS = 10;

// Sprint 6's real auth-stub reads this from process.env.JWT_SECRET, with
// this exact string as its fallback. This is what lets this service's
// tokens be accepted by the SAME mission service, unchanged, without
// either side's code needing to know about the other.
export const JWT_SECRET = process.env.JWT_SECRET || "mission-control-shared-secret-key-32-bytes-minimum";

@Injectable()
export class AuthService {
  private readonly users = new Map<string, StoredUser>();

  constructor() {
    // alice/mission123/MISSION_OPERATOR - matches Sprint 6's auth-stub
    // exactly: same username, same password, same role claim, so a
    // token from THIS service authenticates identically to a token
    // from the stub it replaces.
    void this.register("alice", "mission123", ["MISSION_OPERATOR"]);
  }

  async register(
    username: string,
    password: string,
    roles: string[] = ["MISSION_OPERATOR"],
  ): Promise<{ username: string; registered: true }> {
    if (this.users.has(username)) {
      throw new ConflictException(`${username} is already registered`);
    }
    const passwordHash = await bcrypt.hash(password, SALT_ROUNDS);
    this.users.set(username, { passwordHash, roles, refreshToken: null });
    return { username, registered: true };
  }

  async login(username: string, password: string): Promise<{ accessToken: string; refreshToken: string }> {
    const user = this.users.get(username);
    const passwordMatches = user ? await bcrypt.compare(password, user.passwordHash) : false;
    if (!user || !passwordMatches) {
      throw new UnauthorizedException("invalid username or password");
    }
    const accessToken = this.issueAccessToken(username, user.roles);
    const refreshToken = randomBytes(32).toString("hex");
    user.refreshToken = refreshToken;
    logAuthEvent("login_success", username);
    return { accessToken, refreshToken };
  }

  refresh(refreshToken: string): { accessToken: string } {
    const entry = this.findByRefreshToken(refreshToken);
    if (!entry) {
      throw new UnauthorizedException("invalid or expired refresh token");
    }
    const [username, user] = entry;
    return { accessToken: this.issueAccessToken(username, user.roles) };
  }

  private issueAccessToken(username: string, roles: string[]): string {
    return jwt.sign({ sub: username, roles }, JWT_SECRET, {
      algorithm: "HS256",
      expiresIn: "15m",
    });
  }

  private findByRefreshToken(refreshToken: string): [string, StoredUser] | undefined {
    return [...this.users.entries()].find(([, u]) => u.refreshToken === refreshToken);
  }
}
Quiz hint

Be ready to explain the difference between decoding and verifying, why payload data is visible without a secret, and why a refresh token staying opaque is a feature rather than an omission.

Not every leg of the trip is the same. Access token: short-lived, self-contained, signed. Refresh token: long-lived, server-tracked, revocable.
2

Securing and Testing the Service: lightweight pass, high-value fixes

This module is intentionally narrow. It is not a full security audit. It focuses on the mistakes that bite hardest in practice and a small Jest suite that verifies the core paths.

Pitfall 1: logging secrets

The classic “just log the request body for debugging” mistake captures the password alongside the username and leaves it in logs that may outlive the actual database row.

The pitfall 
const loginAttempt = {{
  username: "alice",
  password: "mission123"
}};

console.log("login attempt:", loginAttempt);

The structural fix

The logger function simply has no parameter for a password or token. That means a rushed developer cannot accidentally pass one through.

logger.ts 
// A minimal stand-in for a real structured logger (pino/winston in
// production). The point of this file isn't the logging library - it's
// the DISCIPLINE of what's allowed to reach it: this function's signature
// makes it impossible to accidentally pass a password or token through,
// because there is no parameter for either.
export function logAuthEvent(event: string, username: string): void {
  console.log(`[auth] ${event} username=${username}`);
}

Pitfall 2: weak or hardcoded secrets

A classroom fallback string is acceptable for a demo, but in production the service should fail fast or be clearly configured with a strong environment-provided secret.

JWT secret source 
export const JWT_SECRET =
  process.env.JWT_SECRET ||
  "mission-control-shared-secret-key-32-bytes-minimum";

Focused Jest tests

The tests are intentionally small and direct. There is no need for a full Nest testing module because AuthService has no constructor dependencies.

auth.service.spec.ts 
import { AuthService, JWT_SECRET } from "./auth.service";
import * as jwt from "jsonwebtoken";

describe("AuthService", () => {
  let service: AuthService;

  beforeEach(() => {
    service = new AuthService();
  });

  it("logs in and receives a valid access token and refresh token", async () => {
    await service.register("carol", "mission123", ["MISSION_OPERATOR"]);
    const { accessToken, refreshToken } = await service.login("carol", "mission123");
    expect(typeof accessToken).toBe("string");
    expect(typeof refreshToken).toBe("string");
    expect(accessToken).not.toEqual(refreshToken);
  });

  it("issues an access token that validates and carries the right claims", async () => {
    await service.register("carol", "mission123", ["MISSION_OPERATOR"]);
    const { accessToken } = await service.login("carol", "mission123");
    const decoded = jwt.verify(accessToken, JWT_SECRET) as jwt.JwtPayload;
    expect(decoded.sub).toBe("carol");
    expect(decoded.roles).toEqual(["MISSION_OPERATOR"]);
  });

  it("rejects login with an incorrect password", async () => {
    await service.register("carol", "mission123", ["MISSION_OPERATOR"]);
    await expect(service.login("carol", "wrong-password")).rejects.toThrow();
  });
});

What these tests prove

  • Successful login returns two distinct strings: access token and refresh token
  • The access token really verifies with jwt.verify()
  • The decoded claims carry the expected sub and roles
  • Incorrect passwords are rejected instead of silently returning null

This is confidence, not completeness. It is the smallest useful safety net around the auth service’s core logic.

“I like me.”
Keep the page warm and human, but keep the auth service disciplined.
Quiz hint

Expect questions on what must never be logged, why a logger API can enforce good behavior structurally, and why new AuthService() inside beforeEach is enough for this particular Jest suite.

3

Mission Build: OpenAPI docs and replacing the Sprint 7 stub

The final module makes the service self-describing and then proves it can stand in for the earlier Java-facing auth stub without changing the Java service at all.

DTO annotations

Add @ApiProperty to fields so the docs show examples and descriptions instead of anonymous objects.

Controller annotations

Add @ApiTags, @ApiOperation and @ApiResponse so the route groups and status codes are documented from the code itself.

Swagger bootstrap

Wire SwaggerModule in main.ts and expose the docs UI at /api.

Replacement proof

Use a real JWT from this service against the unchanged Spring Boot mission service and confirm the side effects in Postgres.

DTO documentation example

login.dto.ts - completed 
import { IsString, IsNotEmpty } from "class-validator";
import { ApiProperty } from "@nestjs/swagger";

export class LoginDto {
  @ApiProperty({
    example: "alice",
    description: "The username to authenticate"
  })
  @IsString()
  @IsNotEmpty()
  username!: string;

  @ApiProperty({
    example: "mission123",
    description: "The plaintext password submitted at login"
  })
  @IsString()
  @IsNotEmpty()
  password!: string;
}

The same pattern applies to RegisterDto so the generated schema and examples are understandable to other developers.

Controller documentation example

auth.controller.ts - completed 
import {
  Body, Controller, Post, HttpCode
} from "@nestjs/common";
import {
  ApiTags, ApiOperation, ApiResponse
} from "@nestjs/swagger";
import { AuthService } from "./auth.service";
import { LoginDto } from "./login.dto";
import { RegisterDto } from "./register.dto";

@ApiTags("auth")
@Controller("auth")
export class AuthController {
  constructor(
    private readonly authService: AuthService
  ) {}

  @ApiOperation({ summary: "Register a new user" })
  @ApiResponse({ status: 201, description: "User registered" })
  @ApiResponse({ status: 409, description: "Username already exists" })
  @Post("register")
  register(@Body() body: RegisterDto) {
    return this.authService.register(
      body.username,
      body.password
    );
  }

  @ApiOperation({ summary: "Authenticate and receive tokens" })
  @ApiResponse({ status: 200, description: "Login success" })
  @ApiResponse({ status: 401, description: "Invalid credentials" })
  @Post("login")
  @HttpCode(200)
  login(@Body() body: LoginDto) {
    return this.authService.login(
      body.username,
      body.password
    );
  }
}

Swagger wiring

main.ts - SwaggerModule 
import "reflect-metadata";
import { NestFactory } from "@nestjs/core";
import { ValidationPipe } from "@nestjs/common";
import {
  DocumentBuilder,
  SwaggerModule
} from "@nestjs/swagger";
import { AppModule } from "./app.module";

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);

  app.useGlobalPipes(
    new ValidationPipe({
      whitelist: true,
      forbidNonWhitelisted: true
    })
  );

  const config = new DocumentBuilder()
    .setTitle("Sprint 8 Auth Service")
    .setDescription(
      "Register, login and token-based auth endpoints"
    )
    .setVersion("1.0")
    .build();

  const document =
    SwaggerModule.createDocument(app, config);

  SwaggerModule.setup("api", app, document);

  await app.listen(3000);
}

Operational routes versus contract routes

The health endpoint exists for readiness checks, but it is intentionally excluded from the public API document.

health.controller.ts 
import { Controller, Get } from "@nestjs/common";
import { ApiExcludeController } from "@nestjs/swagger";

// Excluded from the OpenAPI document itself - it's operational plumbing
// (container readiness checks), not part of the auth service's public
// contract.
@ApiExcludeController()
@Controller()
export class HealthController {
  @Get("health")
  health() {
    return { status: "up" };
  }
}
Contract-first, from the other direction: instead of starting with a hand-written OpenAPI file and generating code, this module starts with code and generates an OpenAPI document from the decorators. The discipline is still the same: the contract stays explicit.
The end-to-end proof matters: the real win is not that Swagger UI appears. The real win is that a token issued by this service authenticates successfully against the completely unmodified Spring Boot mission service because both services agree on the shared secret and claims shape.

Core source map for the final stretch

These are the important files students should recognize by the end of this part of the course.

Auth service

The heart of the app: registration, login, bcrypt checks, JWT issuance, refresh-token storage and lookup.

Auth controller

The HTTP front door exposing register and login, later decorated for OpenAPI generation.

Main bootstrap

The place where ValidationPipe and then SwaggerModule are wired into the application lifecycle.

Final course arc: from DTO validation and auth skeletons, to secure storage and signed tokens, to documentation and integration proof. At this point the service is no longer a teaching stub; it behaves like a small real auth service.
Signed tokens. Cleaner logs. Tested paths. Documented endpoints. This final leg completes the auth service: JWT issuance and verification are real, security mistakes are narrowed, the core paths are covered with tests, and the API documents itself while still authenticating seamlessly with the unchanged Java mission service.
